quick.summary: How to name design tokens so they never break when brands update.
quick.takeaway: Name parts by their job, not their look. Scaling becomes a single click.

parts.title: Name by purpose

beats.line: We changed our brand. Do I really have to rename fifty blue tokens?
Imagine a parking space. It says reserved for the manager, not the red car.
Because the manager might buy a silver car next week.
Exactly. Name things by their job, not their look.
If you name a token blue, it breaks when the brand goes green.
Can I just say name by purpose?
Name by purpose. A primary button stays primary, whatever the color.
That makes sense. But what about the spacing and the layout parts?

parts.cliff: How spacing tokens keep layouts tight.

beats.line: Spacing needs the same logic. Do not name a gap sixteen.
Think of clothing sizes. You buy a medium shirt, not a twenty inch chest.
So I should use small, medium, and large for my spacing?
Exactly. It gives your team a shared language to build with.
If the team decides to increase the medium gap, everything updates.
No one has to hunt down every sixteen pixel margin.
A design system is meant to scale. Hard values slow you down.
So I build with intent, like medium gap and primary color.
And future updates take one click instead of a thousand.

quiz.question: Which of these is the most durable name for a design token?
quiz.explanation: Naming it by purpose ensures it remains accurate even if the actual color value changes.

quiz.question: Hardcoded values scale better than semantic tokens.
quiz.explanation: Hard values force you to update every instance manually. Tokens allow sweeping updates instantly.
